news.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
paras: When people were forced to stay home during COVID‑19, the number of wildfires worldwide fell by about twelve percent. This drop happened because fewer people worked in forests and many grew‑up gardens. Fewer fires mean better air and safer homes for animals and humans alike. But once lockdowns ended, fire activity jumped again, showing people’s habits control the planet. Scientists study these changes to protect forests, plan fire seasons and keep air clean.

news.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
paras: A satisfying ending SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there’s a catch It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX's Starship descends towards the mechanical tower catch at Starbase, Texas on November 14, 2026.

Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

news.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile
paras: The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. on a clear night with no strong winds.

When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together.

news.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
paras: But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

news.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
paras: The dramatic brightening was caused by an outburst on the comet that dumped billions of pounds of dust into space. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004.

It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes.
